title: Microbial Ecology: Introduction into Data Analysis
text:
Introduction
Research projects often generate data that is too big for a spreadsheet or spread over hundreds of files. The command line lets you work with large files and automate repetitive steps, and a High Performance Computer (HPC) lets you run analyses that are too slow for a laptop. This course will teach you how to use these tools: you analyse the 16S rRNA gene data from a Nanopore sequencing run and turn it into a count table of microbial taxa.
This course is designed for students in microbial ecology with little or no prior experience using the command line. During this tutorial, you will learn how to:

title: 1  Setting up a terminal
text:
1.1 Terminology
The command-line interface (CLI) is an alternative to a graphical user interface (GUI) that you probably know better. Both let you work with your computer but in different ways:
When people talk about the CLI, you will hear the words terminal, shell and prompt. They are related but not the same:

title: 1  Setting up a terminal
text:
In a GUI, you click buttons, open folders, and use menus
In the CLI, you type text to issue commands (instructions to your computer) and you see the result as text



The terminal is the window in which you type commands. It is sometimes also called console.
The shell is the program that reads the commands you type in the terminal and tells the operating system what to do. There are several types of shells, for example, bash or zsh. They use slightly different rules, but the basic commands are the same. This course uses bash.
A prompt is the text that the shell shows when it is ready for the next command. It often shows your user name, the name of your computer and the folder you are in. It usually ends with a $ or % sign, for example user@laptop:~$

title: 1  Setting up a terminal
text:
1.2 Installation guides

1.2.1 Windows
Unlike macOS or Linux, Windows doesn’t include a Unix-style terminal by default, so you will need to install one of the following:

MobaXterm (recommended)

Provides a terminal with Linux-like commands built-in
Installation guide: MobaXterm setup instructions. This is a guide from another university, you only need the “Installation instructions” and “Open a terminal”
Easiest option for beginners and lightweight to install
The Home Edition comes in two versions: the installer edition and the portable edition. The installer edition is preferred since with the portable version your home folder is deleted every time you close the application.
After you install it, open MobaXterm and click on Start local terminal.

Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)

Gives you a full Linux environment directly on Windows
Recommended if you’re comfortable installing software or already have some command-line experience
Uses Ubuntu by default, which includes Bash and all standard Linux tools
Installation guide: Microsoft WSL install instructions




1.2.2 Mac
Every Mac comes with a terminal. You do not need to install anything. To open it, do one of these:

In Finder, go to Go → Utilities, then open Terminal.
Or press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight, type Terminal and press Return.

Newer Macs (macOS Catalina and later) use zsh as their shell, not bash. That is fine. Almost everything in this tutorial works the same way in zsh.


1.2.3 Linux
Every Linux system comes with a terminal, and the shell is usually bash. You do not need to install anything. Open the terminal from your applications menu, or search for “Terminal” (depending on your system it can also be called Konsole or xterm).

title: 1  Setting up a terminal
text:
1.3 Sanity check

1.3.1 Check 1: Test your terminal
When the terminal is open, you should see a window with a prompt, similar to the one below. Your prompt will show your own user name and computer name, and the colors may be different.

Type the command below in your terminal and press Enter. Type it exactly as it is shown. Capital letters matter.

# Print the name of the shell you are using
echo $SHELL

Lines that start with # are comments. They explain the code and you do not need to type them. echo prints text to the screen. $SHELL stands for the name of the shell you use, so together they print that name.
On my computer (WSL with Ubuntu) this prints:
/bin/bash
Your output may look a bit different. What matters is that you see a line that ends with bash or zsh (for example /bin/zsh on a newer Mac). If you see this, your terminal works and Check 1 is complete.


1.3.2 Check 2: Test if you can log in to Crunchomics
Crunchomics is the HPC you can use at the UvA, a large computer you can connect and work with from your laptop. We use it later in the course for the analysis. We already organized that you get access to Crunchomics and here we check that the setup worked.
Your network
You can only connect to Crunchomics from the UvA network:

At the UvA, use the eduroam Wi-Fi. The open Amsterdam Science Park Wi-Fi does not work.
From home or anywhere else, connect to the UvA VPN first. If you have not set up the VPN, or it does not work, contact the UvA ICT service desk.

To log in to Crunchomics, type the command below. Replace uvanetid with your own UvAnetID, and press Enter.

ssh -X uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl

What the parts mean:

ssh (secure shell) is the command that connects your terminal to another computer.
-X lets programs on Crunchomics open a window on your screen, for example to show a picture.
uvanetid@ tells Crunchomics who you are.
omics-h0.science.uva.nl is the address of the computer you connect to.

Two things that surprise most people the first time:

The first time you connect, you may get a question that ends with Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?. Type yes and press Enter. Your computer then remembers Crunchomics and does not ask again.
Then you are asked for your password. Use your UvA password. While you type the password, nothing appears on the screen. No dots, no stars. That is normal. Type the password and press Enter.

If the login works, you see a welcome message similar to the one below, and the prompt changes. It now shows your UvAnetID and omics-h0, the name of the Crunchomics computer.

Every command you type now runs on Crunchomics, not on your laptop. For now, log out again:

# Log out of Crunchomics and return to your own laptop
exit

The prompt changes back to the one of your laptop. Check 2 is done.
If the login does not work
Check this first:

Did you type your UvAnetID correctly, and is there an @ between your UvAnetID and the address?
Did you use the correct UvA password? Remember that nothing appears while you type it.
Are you on eduroam (at the UvA) or connected to the VPN (outside the UvA)?

If this still does not work, tell your teachers.

title: 2  Documenting your code
text:
2.1 What the tutorial asks you to write down
You already keep a notebook for this course in which you document your lab work and analyse your data in R. In this tutorial, you also use it for your analysis on the command line: the commands you run, why you run them, and what you see. You hand in your notebook before your presentation, and your teachers read it to prepare their questions.
Good notes also help you: a command that makes sense today can be completely unclear in a few weeks. With clear notes, you, a fellow student or your teachers can see what you did and why, and run it again.
From the chapter “Working on an HPC” on, blue notebook boxes tell you what to add to your notebook. Some boxes have a ‘Compare with my notes’ part. Write your own notes first, then open it. By doing this you will not only document your commands but also learn other good documentation habits:
Some boxes ask you to add these sections to your notebook:

title: 2  Documenting your code
text:
2.2 Code blocks in your notebook
Your notebook is a Quarto (.qmd) or R Markdown (.Rmd) file. In both, a code block starts and ends with three backticks. Watch out: a backtick (`) is not the same as a single quote (’). On many keyboards it is at the top left, below Esc. What you write right after the first three backticks decides what happens to the code:
```bash
# This block is only shown. It is not run.
ls data
```

```{bash}
# This block is run when you render your notebook.
ls data
```

```{r}
# This R block is also run when you render your notebook.
1 + 1
```
For the commands from this tutorial, always use ```bash, without curly brackets. These commands run on Crunchomics, in a project folder that does not exist on your own computer. In a ```{bash} block, your notebook would try to run them on your computer when you render it, and stop with an error.
Use ```{r} for R code that you run yourself, for example when you analyse your count table.

2.3 Markdown basics
The text around your code blocks is written in Markdown. These are the basics you need most:







You type
You get




# Heading, ## Smaller heading
headings (leave a space after the #)


- item at the start of a line
a bullet point


1. item at the start of a line
a numbered list


**bold**, *italic*
bold, italic


`ls -l`

[link text](https://quarto.org)
a link


![](path/to/figure.png)
a figure



Leave an empty line before a heading, a list and a code block. Otherwise, Markdown may not recognise them.
Notice that # means something different in two places. In normal text, it starts a heading. Inside a code block, it starts a comment.
Markdown Basics on the Quarto website lists everything else you can do with Markdown.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.1 pwd: Find out where you are
To get started, open your terminal, and get yourself oriented by typing your first command and then pressing enter:
pwd
The command pwd stands for print working directory. It tells you where you currently are in the file system, that is, which folder (directory) your shell is operating on right now. You should see something like this:

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
/home/username






TipTip: Finding the Desktop on Different Systems





Your home directory (i.e. the directory you start in whenever you open the terminal) varies slightly across operating systems. Here’s how to locate yourself and connect to familiar locations like the Desktop:
macOS

Your home directory is /Users/username
To open the folder you are currently in Finder: open .
Your desktop is at /Users/username/Desktop

MobaXterm (Windows)

Your home directory is /home/mobaxterm
When using the portable version of Mobaxterm this directory is temporary and is deleted when you close MobaXterm. To make it permanent:

Go to Settings –> Configuration –> General
Under Persistent home directory, choose a folder of your choice

To open the folder you are currently in the Windows File explorer: explorer.exe .
Your Desktop is usually at: /mnt/c/Users/username/Desktop or /mnt/c/Users/username/OneDrive/Desktop (when using OneDrive)

WSL2 (Windows)

Your home directory is /home/username
To open the folder you are currently in the Windows File explorer: explorer.exe .
Your Desktop is usually at: /mnt/c/Users/username/Desktop or /mnt/c/Users/username/OneDrive/Desktop (when using OneDrive)

If you want to access the UvA OneDrive folder and/or if your OneDrive folder name includes spaces (like OneDrive - UvA), use quotes around the path:

cd "/mnt/c/Users/username/OneDrive - UvA"

title: 3  Navigating the command line
section: 3.2 ls: List the contents of a directory
text:
3.2 ls: List the contents of a directory
Now that you know where you are, let’s find out what is inside that location, i.e. what files and folders can be found there. The command ls (short for list) shows the files and folders in your current directory. Type the following and press enter:

ls

You should see something like this (your output will vary depending on what’s in your directory):

The colors and formatting depend on your terminal settings, but typically:

Folders (directories) appear in one color (often green or blue)
Files appear in another (often white or bold)

If your directory contains many items, the output can quickly become overwhelming. To make sense of it, you can use options and arguments to control how commands behave.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.3 The structure of a command
A command generally has three parts:

A command name: the program you want to run, i.e. ls
An option (or flag): a way to modify how the command behaves, e.g. -l shows the list in long format, with more details. Options usually start with a -
An argument: the input the command works on, e.g. a file or folder. Some commands work without an argument


Try the following command in your current directory to “List (ls) the contents of the current folder and show details in long format (-l)”:

ls -l

After running this, you see your files and folders again but as a more detailed list. In the example below you can now see additional information about who is allowed to read and change the files (the access modes that determine exactly who can do what to a file or folder), who owns them, how large the files are, when they were last modified and of course their name:







TipTip: Using ls in practice





Throughout this tutorial, you’ll notice that you will use ls frequently. There is a reason for that:
When working with data, sanity checks are essential, because it is easy to make mistakes, overwrite files, or lose track of where things are. Using simple commands like ls, pwd, wc, or grep helps you verify what is happening to your files at every step of an analysis workflow.
These habits are not just for beginners. Bioinformaticians rely on them constantly.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.4 Getting help
At some point, you’ll want to know what options a command has or how it works. In this case, you should first check if manual pages (or man pages) are available for the command by typing man followed by the command name:

man pwd

This opens the manual entry for the command pwd. You can scroll through it using:

↑ / ↓ arrows or the space bar to move down
b to move back up
q to quit the manual

MobaXterm users: MobaXterm does not come with manual pages, so man pwd does not work. Use pwd --help instead (see below). If one way gives an error, try the next.
Not all commands come with such a manual. Depending on the program, there are a few common patterns you can try to get help:

man pwd
pwd --help
pwd -h

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.5 mkdir: Make a new folder
Before you start moving around, let’s first learn how to create new folders (also called directories). This is something you will do often, for example, to keep raw data, results, and scripts organized in separate places. The command you use for that is mkdir, which stands for make directory.
For now, you will use mkdir to create a project folder with the name data_analysis for this tutorial. Don’t worry about how to move into the folder yet. You will learn that in the next section.

# Move into the home directory (the starting point of your system)
cd ~

# Create a new folder called 'data_analysis'
mkdir data_analysis

# Check that the folder was created successfully
ls

You should see that a new folder called data_analysis appears in the list. You will use this folder as your project folder for all exercises in this tutorial. Next, let’s make a new data folder inside the new data_analysis folder by typing the following:

# Make a data folder inside the data_analysis folder
# The `-p` option makes the parent directory (here: data_analysis), if it does not already exist
# It is useful to add `-p` when generating a folder inside a folder
mkdir -p data_analysis/data

# Check that the folder was created successfully
# Notice here how you use ls with a flag and also with an optional argument?
ls -l data_analysis

You can also look at the folder you are currently in via the file browser you know from Windows or Mac. The command below opens the folder you are in right now. The dot (.) is short for “the current folder”:

# Windows (MobaXterm or WSL2): open the current folder in File Explorer
explorer.exe .

# Mac: open the current folder in Finder
open .







TipTip: Commenting your code





Notice how I added # and some notes above each command?
Anything written after # in Bash is a comment. A comment won’t be executed, but it helps you (and others) understand what the command does.
In your own work, add short, meaningful comments above key steps. Avoid restating the obvious. Instead, explain why you’re doing something or what it achieves.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.6 cd: Move around folders
Now that you have your own project folder, you will learn how to move around the file system with cd (short for change directory).
The file system is structured like a tree that starts from a single root directory, written as a forward slash (/). All other folders branch out from this root directory. For example, you can go from the root directory to the home folder, and from there into the folder with your user name.

The location of a file or folder is written as a path: the folder names along the way, separated by /, e.g. /home/username. There are two ways to write a path, for example to the data folder:

An absolute path starts from the root, e.g. cd /home/username/data_analysis/data
A relative path starts from your current location, e.g. cd data if you are already in /home/username/data_analysis

It is generally recommended to use relative paths from inside your project folder. That makes your code more portable: it still works if you move the project folder or run it on another computer.
Let’s practice moving between folders. At each step, use pwd if you feel that you get lost:

# Move into the data analysis folder 
cd data_analysis 

# Check where you are 
pwd

You now should see something like /home/username/data_analysis. You can use the cd command in multiple ways to move around:

# Move into the data folder
cd data

# Move one level up (..), i.e. go back to the data_analysis folder
cd ..

# Quickly go back home (you now should be in the home directory)
cd ~

# Move multiple levels down at once
cd data_analysis/data

# Move two levels up and go back into the home directory
cd ../.. 

# And go back to the data_analysis folder 
cd data_analysis

In the code above, the tilde symbol (~) is a shortcut for your home directory. It is the same as typing the full absolute path to your home (e.g. cd /home/username), but much faster to type. Two dots (..) always mean “the folder one level up”.






TipTip: Command-line completion





Here are some tips for faster navigation (and fewer typos):

Use the Tab key for autocompletion: type the first few letters of a folder or file name and press Tab. For example, go to your home directory, type cd data_ and press Tab. The shell fills in data_analysis for you. Then press Enter.
If there is more than one match, the shell cannot decide which one you mean. Press Tab twice to see all options.
Use the ↑ / ↓ arrow keys to scroll through commands you ran before. This is useful to rerun a command or to change a small part of it.

From now on, try to use the Tab key often, so that you do not have to type everything yourself.









QuestionTask





Familiarize yourself with these first commands and:

Move into the results folder and confirm your location with pwd
Move back inside the data_analysis folder
Use ls to confirm both results and data are there

pwd

title: 3  Navigating the command line
section: 3.7 Error messages and Ctrl+C: Getting unstuck
text:
3.7 Error messages and Ctrl+C: Getting unstuck
Let’s make a mistake on purpose. From inside your data_analysis folder, list a folder with a typo in its name:

# A typo on purpose: the folder is called data, not dta
ls -l dta

This prints something like this:
ls: cannot access 'dta': No such file or directory
An error message is how the shell tells you what went wrong. Read it from left to right:

ls: the command that ran into a problem
cannot access 'dta': what it tried to do, and with which file or folder
No such file or directory: why it did not work

The exact wording can be a bit different on your system, but you will find the same three parts.
No such file or directory is the error you will see most often. It usually has one of three causes:

There is a typo in the name. Use the Tab key, so that the shell fills in names for you.
You are in a different folder than you think. Check with pwd and ls.
The file does not exist yet, for example because an earlier step did not work.

If you make a typo in the name of the command itself, for example lss instead of ls, the message contains command not found. The shell does not know a command with that name.
Sometimes a command does not finish, or you start something by mistake. The prompt does not come back, and you can’t type a new command. Press Ctrl+C (also on a Mac) to stop the command and get your prompt back. Note that Ctrl+C does not close man or less. For these tools press q to quit them.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.8 wget: Download data
Next, let’s download a fasta file that contains the sequence of a 16S rRNA gene of one of the strains you used in the lab. This file will be useful to learn about some other commands. Below, you use the wget command to fetch a fasta file from an online website as follows:

# Download the example fasta file into the current directory
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz







ImportantWget for Mac users



For Mac users wget is not installed by default. If you do not want to install it, you can instead use the curl command:

# -O: save the file under its original name
# -L: Tells curl that if the server tells it to go somewhere else, follow it until you reach the actual file
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz



After you download any kind of data, it is always a good idea to do a sanity check: is the file there, and how large is it? A file size of 0 means that something went wrong during the download.

# List files in long (-l) and human-readable (-h) format
# combining these two options becomes -lh
# You should see that the file exists and is not empty
ls -lh LjRoot303.fasta.gz

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.9 cp: Copy files
cp (short for copy) duplicates files or folders. When working with many files, a good folder structure is essential to keep track of files (useful folders are, for example, data, scripts and results).
Let’s use cp to copy the downloaded file into data and to organize the data a bit better:

# Copy the file into data 
cp LjRoot303.fasta.gz data/

# Show the content of both locations
ls -l
ls -l data

When running the two ls commands, you see that you now have two copies of LjRoot303.fasta.gz, one file is in your working directory and the other one is in your data folder. Having large files in multiple locations is not ideal since you use unnecessary space. However, you can use another command to move the file into your data folder instead of copying it.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.10 mv: Move (or rename) files
mv (short for move) moves files or folders to a new location without creating a second copy:

# Move the file into data
mv LjRoot303.fasta.gz data/

# Verify
ls -l
ls -l data

Notice that mv moved the file and, without asking and without showing, overwrote the copy that you had put into the data folder with cp (you would only know that if you carefully tracked the modification date of the file). So whenever you use mv, make sure that you do not overwrite files by mistake.
mv is also the command to rename a file: you “move” it to a new name, e.g. mv old_name.txt new_name.txt.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.11 rm: Remove files and directories
To remove files and folders, you use the rm command. For example, you could remove the LjRoot303.fasta.gz in case you don’t need it anymore:

# Remove the fasta file from the data folder
rm data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz

# Check if that worked
ls -l data

If you want to remove a folder, you need to tell rm that you want to remove folders using an option. To do this, you use -r (short for recursive), which removes a folder together with everything inside it.






Important



Unix does not have an undelete command.
This means that if you delete something with rm, it’s gone. Therefore, use rm with care and check what you write twice before pressing enter!
Also, NEVER run rm -r or rm -rf (-f: “force: don’t ask, don’t complain”) on the root / folder or any important path. Always double check the path or file name before pressing enter when using the rm command.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.12 gzip: (Un)compress files
You might have noticed that the file you downloaded ends with .gz. This extension is used for files that are compressed to make the file smaller. This is useful for saving files and saving space, but this makes the file unreadable for a human. To be able to learn how to read the content of a file, let’s learn how to uncompress the file first.

# Download the LjRoot303.fasta.gz file again 
# Here, you use the -P option to directly download the file into the data folder 
wget -P data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz

# Check that this worked 
# You now should see two files
ls -l data

# Uncompress the file with gzip 
# Here, you use -d to decompress the file 
# (by default gzip will compress a file)
gzip -d data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz 

# Check that this worked 
# You now should see that one file is uncompressed (i.e. it lost the gz extension)
ls data







ImportantWget -P for Mobaxterm users



Mobaxterm by default comes with a wget version with less functionality and you might see the error “wget: Unknown option P”. To solve this, you can install a newer version as follows (or use the curl command):

apt-get install wget









ImportantWget -P for Mac users



For Mac users that use curl instead of wget, you can redirect the file to a specific folder like this:

curl --output-dir data -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/LjRoot303.fasta.gz

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.13 Exploring file contents
Now that you have the uncompressed file, you can use different ways to explore the content of a file.

3.13.1 cat: Print the full file
You can use cat to print the entire file to the screen. This is useful for smaller files, but can get overwhelming for long ones, where you would see hundreds of lines just flying over the screen.

cat data/LjRoot303.fasta



3.13.2 head and tail: View parts of a file
To only print the first few or last few lines, you can use the head and tail commands:

# Show the first 10 lines
head data/LjRoot303.fasta

# Show the last 5 lines
# Here, the option -n lets you control how many lines get printed
tail -n 5 data/LjRoot303.fasta



3.13.3 less: View the full file
less lets you view a file’s contents one screen at a time. This is useful when dealing with a large text file (such as a sequence data file) because it doesn’t load the entire file but accesses it page by page, resulting in fast loading speeds.

less -S data/LjRoot303.fasta

The option -S keeps each long line on one line on the screen, instead of continuing it on the next line. Inside less, you can:

Use the → / ← arrow keys to see the rest of a long line
Move up and down with the ↑ / ↓ arrow keys, or with Page Up / Page Down
Press q to quit



3.13.4 zcat: Decompress and print to screen
When you used gzip above, you decompressed the file and that allowed you to read the content of the fasta file. This is perfect for smaller files, but not ideal for sequence data since these files get large and you might not want to decompress these files as they would clutter your system.
Luckily, there is one useful tool in bash to decompress the file and print the content to the screen. zcat will print the content of a file to the screen but leave the file as is.

# Check the content of the data folder 
# You should have one compressed and one uncompressed file 
ls -l data

# Use zcat on the compressed file to view its content
zcat data/GCF_000714595.fasta.gz

# Check the content of the data folder 
# You still should have one compressed and one uncompressed file 
ls -l data







ImportantZcat for Mac users



For Mac users, zcat might not work as expected. Try using gzcat instead:

gzcat data/GCF_000714595.fasta.gz









TipTip: Editing text files with nano





You can also edit the content of a text file and there are different programs available to do this on the command line, one such tool is nano, which should come with most command line interpreters. You can open any file as follows:

nano data/LjRoot303.fasta

Once the document is open you can edit it however you want and then

Close the document with Control + X
Type y to save changes and press enter

MobaXterm users: MobaXterm does not come with nano. Install it once with apt-get install nano.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.14 wc: Count things
Another useful tool is the wc (short for wordcount) command that lets you count the number of lines via -l in a file. It is a useful tool for sanity checking.

wc -l data/LjRoot303.fasta

You see that this file contains 20 lines of text. For fasta files this is not very informative, but if you for example work with a dataframe with rows and columns where you filter rows using certain conditions this can become very useful for sanity checking.

title: 3  Navigating the command line
section: 3.15 grep : print lines that match patterns
text:
3.15 grep : print lines that match patterns
The grep command searches for patterns in a file. You could, for example, use this to ask how many 16S rRNA gene sequences are in your fasta file by searching for the fasta header that always starts with a >. The basic grep syntax is grep "pattern" file. Here, “pattern” is the text you want to search for, and file is the file you want to search in. The double quotes let you include special characters (like >) safely.

grep ">" data/LjRoot303.fasta

This prints all lines that match the pattern (here: >). In a fasta file, > is used to label the sequence headers. Depending on your terminal, the matches might be highlighted, which makes them easy to spot.
If you only want to count the number of headers, you can use the -c option:

# LjRoot303 contains 1 16S rRNA gene sequence
grep -c ">" data/LjRoot303.fasta







TipTip: The structure of sequence files





A sequence FASTA file is a text based format to store DNA or peptide sequences. It should always look something like this:

The header always starts with a > followed by descriptive information. In a new line the sequence data gets stored in either a single line or multiple lines. A fasta file can contain a single sequence or multiple sequences.
By convention the extension .fna is used to store fasta sequences from nucleotides and .faa is used to store fasta sequences from proteins. The extension .fasta can contain either nucleotide or protein sequences.
Another common extension is fastq. Fastq files are used to store sequencing data generated by sequencers and contain four lines of information: (i) the sequence header, (ii) the sequence itself, (iii) a separator and (iv) information about the quality of each single base pair in the sequence. They typically look something like this:










QuestionTask






Uncompress the file for GCF_000714595
Compare the number of 16S rRNA gene sequences for GCF_000714595 and LjRoot303
What could it mean if one microbial species has more 16S rRNA gene sequences than another?







AnswerClick to see the answer






# Uncompress 
gzip -d data/GCF_000714595.fasta.gz

# Count the number of 16S rRNA gene sequences 
# LjRoot303 has 1 and GCF_000714595 has 9 16S rRNA gene sequences
grep -c ">" data/LjRoot303.fasta
grep -c ">" data/GCF_000714595.fasta

Answer for question 3:
Bacteria can carry multiple copies of the rRNA operon (16S–23S–5S). A higher copy number is often associated with fast-responding, fast-growing life strategies (more ribosomes → faster protein synthesis under nutrient-rich conditions).
This can cause problems in, for example, 16S rRNA gene amplicon analyses:

A single organism may produce multiple slightly distinct 16S sequences, inflating apparent diversity
Species with higher 16S copy number will produce more amplicon reads per cell. So raw read counts overestimate their true cell abundance unless you correct for copy number (which is difficult)

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.16 Working with multiple files
So far, you have worked with single files. In practice, sequencing data often comes as multiple files, for example, one file per strain or per sample. Let’s practice handling several files at once. Let’s begin by getting more fasta files and not only download 16S sequences from strains isolated from Lotus japonicus (files with Lj prefix) but also sequences from strains coming from a human background (files with GCF prefix):
Warning: If you downloaded one of the files in the exercise before, then you don’t need to run this wget command again. That is because wget does not overwrite a file that already exists but instead saves a second copy as name.fasta.gz.1. If this happens, delete that copy.

# Download some more data 
wget -P data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/GCF_000009425.fasta.gz
wget -P data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/GCF_000253315.fasta.gz
wget -P data https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/LjRoot59.fasta.gz

# Check what was done
ls -lh data

You now should have 5 files, 3 of which are still compressed.






TipHint: Downloading many files with a for loop





Once you understand how to use wget, you can easily scale it up to download multiple files automatically using a for loop.
First, make a file called accessions.txt in your data_analysis folder. It lists all the accessions that were used in the lab experiments, one accession per line. Open a new, empty file with nano:

nano accessions.txt

MobaXterm users: MobaXterm does not come with nano. Install it once with apt-get install nano.
Copy the list below and paste it into nano (right-click in MobaXterm and WSL, Cmd+V on a Mac):
GCF_000009425
GCF_000253315
GCF_000714595
GCF_002055965
GCF_014058685
LjRoot303
LjRoot44
LjRoot59
LjRoot60
Root401
Root68
Root935
Then save the file and close nano: press Ctrl+X, type y, and press Enter to keep the file name. Check that the file looks right:

# Print the file: you should see 12 accessions, one per line
cat accessions.txt

You can then loop through all accessions in the file and download each file into a new folder called loop_download:

# Make a new folder
mkdir loop_download 

# Download all files at once
for accession in $(cat accessions.txt); do
    wget -P loop_download https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/MicEco_teaching_material/main/data/${accession}.fasta.gz
done

# Check that the download worked: you should see 12 files
ls -lh loop_download

Here’s what happens:

$(cat accessions.txt) reads all lines from the file
for accession in ... goes through each line one by one and stores an accession name in the accession variable
wget -P loop_download github_path/${accession}.fasta.gz downloads the compressed fasta file for each accession into the loop_download folder. Here, the ${accession} will get replaced with one line in accessions.txt

You can use this same loop structure to run any command on multiple files automatically. This is one of the main reasons the CLI is so powerful. For example, you could in one command count the number of headers in all your fasta files:

# Count the 16S rRNA gene sequences in each downloaded file
# Mac users: use gzcat instead of zcat
for accession in $(cat accessions.txt); do
    echo $accession
    zcat loop_download/${accession}.fasta.gz | grep -c ">"
done

Here, zcat prints the content of each compressed file, and the | sends that content to grep -c ">", which counts the headers. The | is called a pipe. You will learn more about pipes at the end of this page.
You can also format this more nicely if you really want to but this is outside of the scope of this tutorial. A more detailed explanation about for-loops can be found here.




3.16.1 Wildcards (*): Match multiple files
Imagine you want to uncompress all the new files. Typing a gzip command for every file will get tedious and you risk mistyping names.
Luckily, the shell provides special characters to work with groups of files using pattern matching. These characters are called wildcards. The most useful wildcard is *, which stands for “any characters, any number of times (also zero times)”. For example, *.txt matches all files that end with .txt.

# List all files inside the data folder that end with gz
# You should see only 3 files
ls -l data/*gz

# List all uncompressed Lotus fasta files inside the data folder 
# using `Lj*.fasta` means you look for filenames that 
# start with Lj, are followed by any number of characters and end with .fasta
ls -l data/Lj*.fasta

You can use wildcards with every bash command and, for example, use them to uncompress every file at once:

gzip -d data/*gz

# Check if that worked
ls -lh data



3.16.2 cat and > : Combining and saving files
The cat command doesn’t just print files, it can also concatenate (join) multiple files into one. For example, you might want to combine all fasta sequences for the Lotus (Lj) strains and store the output in a new file called lotus.fasta in the results folder (a folder you should have generated in an earlier exercise).

# Combine the Lotus fasta files into one 
# and store the output of the cat command in a new file 
cat data/Lj*.fasta > results/lotus.fasta

Here:

cat data/Lj*.fasta selects all files in the data folder that start with Lj and end with .fasta.
> tells the shell to write the combined output into a new file that will be called lotus.fasta

When you run this command nothing gets printed and the output goes into the file results/lotus.fasta.






CautionImportant: Be careful with >





The > operator overwrites files without asking. If you want to add (append) to an existing file instead of replacing it, use >>.



Whenever you combine or modify files it is a good idea to do some sanity checks. Luckily, you already learned about useful ways to do this:

# Check how many 16S sequences are found in individual Lotus strains 
grep -c ">" data/Lj*

# Check how many 16S sequences are in the concatenated file
# Important: the numbers should add up with the numbers from the command above
grep -c ">" results/lotus.fasta







QuestionQuestion






Combine the 16S rRNA gene sequences from human-associated strains (GCF Prefix) into a new file and store this file in the results folder
Count the total number of 16S sequences in the individual and the combined file







AnswerClick to see the answer






# Combine
cat data/GCF*.fasta > results/human.fasta

# Count 
grep -c ">" data/GCF*.fasta 
grep -c ">" results/human.fasta

title: 3  Navigating the command line
text:
3.17 Pipes
So far, you have run one command at a time. But often, you might want to combine commands so that the output of one becomes the input of another. That’s what the pipe (|) does. It lets you chain simple commands together to do more complex things.
For example, you might want to ask how many sequences all human-associated strains have together but might not want to store a concatenated file to do so. Here, you could do the following instead:

# Combine all human-associated files and count the total number of 16S sequences
cat data/GCF*.fasta | grep -c ">"

Here:

cat data/GCF*.fasta concatenates fasta files from all human-associated strains
The pipe (|) sends the combined sequences directly to the grep command
grep -c ">" only counts how many headers are found in the combined file

A second common use of the pipe is to show only the first lines of a long output:

# Find all headers and show only the first 3
grep ">" data/GCF_000714595.fasta | head -n 3

Here, grep finds all 9 header lines, and head -n 3 prints only the first 3. Later in this course, you will use the same pattern to look at the start of a large compressed file without uncompressing it: zcat file.fastq.gz | head.

title: 4  HPC introduction
text:
4.1 Storage
If you work at IBED you can get access to Crunchomics, the Genomics Compute Environment for SILS and IBED. Crunchomics is an HPC (high-performance computer): a group of powerful computers that many people share. Your contact person for Crunchomics is Wim de Leeuw (w.c.deleeuw@uva.nl).
Working on an HPC is a bit different from working on your own computer. The figure below gives a simplified overview:
On Crunchomics, you have two folders. In these paths, $USER stands for your UvAnetID. You don’t have to replace it yourself: when you use $USER in a command on Crunchomics, bash fills in your UvAnetID.
Good to know:

title: 4  HPC introduction
text:
Your home directory, /home/$USER, with 25 GB of space
Your personal directory, /zfs/omics/personal/$USER, with 500 GB of space. Since this directory is larger, use it for all your analyses and software. On the next page, you make a shortcut to it, ~/personal, and keep your project folder there



Your data is removed from Crunchomics when your UvAnetID expires
If you need more space, or a shared folder for a larger project with several team members, contact Wim de Leeuw
Crunchomics automatically saves copies of your files, called snapshots:

It makes one every hour, kept for 24 hours, and one every day around midnight, kept for a week
So if you delete a file by mistake, it can be restored for up to a week
But files you delete also still count towards your storage limit for up to a week
To restore a file, or to remove snapshots when you run out of space, contact Wim de Leeuw

Your data is stored on several disks, which protects it if one disk breaks. But it is not copied anywhere else. Crunchomics is not a backup or an archive. You are responsible for backing up your own data. The website of the IBED computational support team explains the archiving options at the UvA

title: 4  HPC introduction
text:
4.2 Compute resources

Crunchomics has 5 compute nodes, each with 64 CPUs and 512 GB of memory
If you need more resources, or GPUs, see the website of the IBED computational support team
You find more information in the Crunchomics documentation







Important



Crunchomics etiquette
You share Crunchomics with many other people, so only ask for the resources that you actually use. There are no hard limits, but please follow these rules:

Do NOT run jobs that need many CPUs or a lot of memory on the login node (omics-h0). Use the compute nodes (omics-cn001 to omics-cn005) for this
Do NOT use more than 20% of the CPUs or memory of the cluster for more than a day. That is about one full compute node. If you have large jobs, contact Wim de Leeuw
Don’t leave resources that you reserved unused, and set reasonable time limits on your jobs
Use the queue (SLURM) for large jobs. Working directly on the login node is possible, but only for small tasks.
Close programs when you don’t use them anymore, for example an R session

You learn how to ask for resources and time on the next page. Please look back at the etiquette rules once you run your own analyses.

5.1 Writing it down in your notebook
Now that you are more comfortable with the command line, you will learn how to work on the UvA Crunchomics HPC. In this section, you will go through the following steps:
You already keep a notebook for your lab work. From now on, you also write down the commands you run, with a comment on what each command does, and a few words about what you saw. At the end of some sections, a blue notebook box tells you what to add. For some of them, you can compare your notes with mine. Your notes don’t have to look like mine, as long as future you understands them.
A few rules for all your notes:

title: 5  Working on an HPC

Put commands in a code block that starts with ```bash and ends with ```. Such a block is only shown in your notebook, it is not run
Your notebook stays on your own computer. Copy the commands from the terminal that is logged in to Crunchomics into it

title: 5  Working on an HPC
text:
5.2 Connecting to the HPC

5.2.1 ssh: Connecting to a server
SSH (Secure Shell) is a way for two computers to connect to each other securely. Here, you use it to connect your computer with the Crunchomics HPC. The general command looks like this:

ssh -X username@server

Here:

username is your account name on the HPC, i.e. your UvAnetID
server is the address of the HPC you want to connect to, for Crunchomics this is omics-h0.science.uva.nl
-X lets programs on Crunchomics open windows, for example a plot, on your own computer

To log in to Crunchomics, use the following command and enter your UvA password when you are asked for it. Remember that nothing appears on the screen while you type your password:

ssh -X uvanetid@omics-h0.science.uva.nl







Important



Important tips for connecting:

If you want to log into Crunchomics while working from UvA use the eduroam network, not the open Amsterdam Science Park network

If you are connecting from outside UvA, you must be on the VPN. Contact ICT if you have not set it up or encounter issues
Always double-check your username and server address to avoid login errors





5.2.2 Crunchomics: Preparing your account
If this is your first time using Crunchomics, you need to run a small Bash script to set up your account. Ignore this section if you have done this before. This script will:

Add /zfs/omics/software/bin to your PATH variable. The PATH is the list of folders in which bash looks for programs. With this change, bash can find the software that is already installed on Crunchomics
Set up a Python 3 environment with some useful Python packages
Create a link called personal in your home directory. This link leads to your personal directory, which has 500 GB of space. Your home directory itself only has 25 GB

To set up your account, run the following commands:

# First orient yourself by typing 
pwd 
ls -lh 

# Run the Crunchomics installation script
/zfs/omics/software/script/omics_install_script

# Check if something changed
# You now should see the personal folder inside your home directory 
ls -lh



5.2.3 conda: Installing your own software
Crunchomics already has a lot of software installed, but not every tool. For example, NanoPlot, the tool that you use to make quality plots of your reads, is not yet installed. You can’t install software into the shared software folders of Crunchomics, because you don’t have administrator rights (the permission to change the software for everyone).
Instead, you use conda: a program that installs software into your own folders, without administrator rights. mamba does the same as conda, but faster. It understands the same commands, so you can swap conda and mamba in almost all commands that you find online.
conda installs each tool into its own environment: a separate folder with the tool and all the other programs it needs, in exactly the right versions. This way, tools that need different versions of the same program don’t get in each other’s way. To use a tool, you activate its environment. Activating adds the environment’s folder to the front of your PATH (the list of folders in which bash looks for programs, see the setup above), so bash finds the tool there first.

5.2.3.1 Install Miniforge
First, check if you already have conda or mamba:

conda --version
mamba --version

If both commands print a version number, conda is already installed, and you can skip to the next section. If you have conda but not mamba, that is fine too: replace mamba with conda in all commands in this tutorial. If both print an error message (for example conda: command not found), install Miniforge, a small installer that contains conda and mamba.






ImportantInstall Miniforge into your personal folder, not into your home folder



Your home folder on Crunchomics has only 25 GB of space, and conda environments can take up several GB once you have a few of them. So you install Miniforge into your personal folder, which has 500 GB: /zfs/omics/personal/$USER/miniforge3.
$USER is a variable: a name that stands for a value. Bash has already set it for you, and it contains your user name. So for you, bash replaces $USER with your UvAnetID. That way, you can copy the commands below exactly as they are.


Installing Miniforge is a small job, so it is fine to run it on the login node. Run the commands one by one:

# Go into your personal folder
cd /zfs/omics/personal/$USER

# Download the Miniforge installer
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"

# Check that the installer was downloaded
ls -lh Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh

# Run the installer
# -b: install without asking any questions
# -p: define the folder to install Miniforge into
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh -b -p /zfs/omics/personal/$USER/miniforge3

# Check that the folder was created
ls /zfs/omics/personal/$USER/miniforge3

Here:

curl -L -O: downloads a file from the internet and saves it under its own name
$(uname)-$(uname -m): fills in the type of computer you work on, so that you download the installer that fits it. On Crunchomics, this becomes Linux-x86_64, so the installer is called Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
-b: runs the installer without questions. Without -b, the installer asks you to read the license and to type the folder for the installation yourself. Typing that folder by hand is easy to get wrong, which is why you give it with -p instead
By using -b, you accept the Miniforge license without seeing it. Have a look at it if you want to know what you agree to

The installer has now put conda into your personal folder, but bash does not know about it yet. The next command adds a few lines to your ~/.bashrc file. This file contains settings that bash reads every time you log in. With these lines, bash can find conda from now on:

# Set up conda for bash (only needed once)
/zfs/omics/personal/$USER/miniforge3/bin/conda init

# Read the new settings without logging out and in again
source ~/.bashrc

# Check that bash now finds conda and mamba
conda --version
mamba --version

conda init prints a long list of files, most of them with “no change”. That is fine. The output also tells you to close and re-open your shell. source ~/.bashrc does the same thing, so you don’t have to log out.
You should now see (base) at the start of your prompt. This shows that conda is active, and that you are in its base environment, the environment that comes with Miniforge.


5.2.3.2 mamba create: Install NanoPlot
NanoPlot is a visualization tool for long-read sequencing data. Let’s install it into a new environment:

# Check if NanoPlot is already available
NanoPlot -h

# If not installed, create a new environment called nanoplot_1.48.0 and install it
# Press Y and Enter when mamba asks you to confirm
mamba create -n nanoplot_1.48.0 -c conda-forge -c bioconda nanoplot=1.48.0 python=3.12

Here:

mamba create: make a new, empty environment
-n nanoplot_1.48.0: the name of the environment. You use this name later to activate the environment. The name includes the version, so you can always see which version you use
-c conda-forge -c bioconda: where mamba looks for the software. These online collections are called channels. Bioconda holds thousands of bioinformatics tools. Conda-forge holds general software that many of these tools need (for example plotting libraries). You can search for tools and versions on anaconda.org
nanoplot=1.48.0: the tool to install, and its exact version. Everyone in the course uses the same version, so everyone gets the same output and the same plots. Without =1.48.0, mamba installs the newest version, which can change between today and next month
python=3.12: the Python version that NanoPlot uses. You fix this version because NanoPlot does not work well with the newest Python

Let’s use the new environment:

# Activate the environment
conda activate nanoplot_1.48.0

# Check which NanoPlot bash finds now, and its version
which NanoPlot
NanoPlot --version

# Leave the environment again
conda deactivate

When the environment is active, you see (nanoplot_1.48.0) at the start of your prompt, and which NanoPlot shows a path inside your miniforge3 folder.
Recommendations:

Keep the base environment clean: make a new environment for each tool, instead of installing everything into base
Always install a specific version (tool=version), and put the version number in the name of the environment. To install a different version, change the number in both places
Check the documentation of a tool for installation notes or version requirements
List all your environments with conda env list
Remove an environment that you no longer need with conda env remove -n name_of_the_environment







NotebookNotebook checkpoint: Project description and software





If your notebook does not have one yet, add a heading ## Project description at the top. Write down your community (which strains), your hypothesis in one or two sentences, and the samples you sequenced. You can add the barcodes later.
Software gets its own place in your notebook: near the top, below the short description of your project. Someone who wants to repeat your analysis then sees right away what they need to install first.
Add a heading ## Software near the top of your notebook, and below it:

Which conda version you are working with and in what folder you installed it
The mamba create command, the name of the environment and the NanoPlot version that NanoPlot --version printed
Add a heading ## Error log at the end of your notebook, also if you had no error yet. Did conda or mamba give you an error? Write down the command, the error message and how you fixed it. Keep this section for all errors you get from now on







Notebook-answerCompare with my notes

- Hypothesis: <one or two sentences>
- Sequenced samples: barcode<NN> (<community, replicate>), barcode<NN> (...)

## Software

On Crunchomics:

- NanoPlot 1.48.0, in the conda environment `nanoplot_1.48.0`

```bash
# On Crunchomics: install NanoPlot into its own environment
mamba create -n nanoplot_1.48.0 -c conda-forge -c bioconda nanoplot=1.48.0 python=3.12
```









5.2.4 Preparing your working directory
Next, you can start organizing your project folder. You always want to generate project folders inside your personal directory, which provides more storage than the home directory:

# Go into the personal folder
cd ~/personal 

# Make and go into a new project folder
mkdir data_analysis
cd data_analysis 

# Ensure that you are in the right folder 
pwd

You now have a clean workspace for all the analyses that you will run during this tutorial on Crunchomics. As in your local machine, it’s good practice to keep your raw data, results, and scripts organized in separate folders.


5.2.5 scp: Transferring data from/to a server
To learn how to transfer data to Crunchomics, you transfer the data folder (the one you made in the previous part of the tutorial) to the HPC. You do this with the scp (Secure Copy Protocol) command, which securely transfers files or directories between your computer and a remote server.
The basic syntax is:

scp [options] SOURCE DESTINATION
For connecting to any HPC the syntax is username@server:path

When transferring data you must run the command from a terminal session on your own computer, not from a terminal session that runs on the HPC. To keep yourself organized it’s often useful to have one terminal session open on your laptop and another one on Crunchomics as shown in the example below:

To copy the entire data folder into your Crunchomics project folder, use:

# On my computer, inside my local data_analysis folder
# Replace 'username' (twice) with your UvAnetID
scp -r data username@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/username/personal/data_analysis

# On Crunchomics, inside ~/personal/data_analysis: check that the files arrived
# ll is a short form of ls -l. It works on Crunchomics, but not on every computer
ll data

Notes:

The -r option copies directories recursively, i.e. it copies a folder together with everything inside it
It’s helpful to keep two terminal windows open: one for your local computer and one for the HPC
Run this command from inside your local data_analysis folder (the one you created earlier)







TipTip: Moving data from the HPC to your own computer





You can also move results from the HPC to your computer. For example, to copy a single genome file from Crunchomics:

# On my computer
scp username@omics-h0.science.uva.nl:/home/username/personal/data_analysis/data/LjRoot303.fasta .

title: 5  Working on an HPC
text:
5.3 Submitting jobs with SLURM
In the HPC introduction, you learned that there are two main “sections” on an HPC:

Login node: where you log in and do light work, such as moving files, editing scripts, or preparing jobs.
Compute nodes: where the actual analyses run. These nodes have more CPUs and memory and are managed by a scheduling system.

To use these compute nodes efficiently, you communicate with them through SLURM, a workload manager that decides when, where, and how your jobs run based on the available resources.

5.3.1 squeue: View info about jobs in the queue
The command below shows you which jobs are currently running or waiting in the queue:

squeue

This displays all jobs submitted to the system, and might look something like this:





Some useful columns to know:

JOBID: a unique number assigned to each job; you can use it to check on a job later.
ST: the current state of the job (e.g., R = running, PD = pending).
A full list of SLURM job state codes can be found here

Once you have submitted a job, it appears in this list as well. To see only your own jobs, add the -u option followed by your user name. Instead of typing your user name, you can use $USER (you already used $USER when you installed Miniforge):

# Check what is stored in the USER variable 
# echo: a command that prints the text you give it to the screen
echo $USER 

# Check if you have any running jobs
squeue -u $USER

Note that if you don’t have any active running jobs, squeue -u $USER will only print the header line.


5.3.2 srun: Submitting a job interactively
Now that you have seen how to check the job queue, let’s learn how to actually run jobs on the compute nodes. There are two main ways to submit jobs: srun and sbatch. This course only needs srun, and sbatch is in a bonus section at the end of this chapter. You typically use srun when:

You want to run tasks interactively and see the output directly on your screen
You are testing a command before you run it on more data
You have short jobs (usually less than a few hours)

Important: Jobs started with srun will stop if you disconnect from the HPC (unless you use tools like screen or tmux, which this tutorial doesn’t cover).
If something goes wrong then you can stop a job that you started with srun by pressing Ctrl+C.
Let’s start with a very simple example to see how srun works:

srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=1G --time=00:10:00 echo "Hello world"

Here’s what each part means:

srun → communicate to SLURM that you want to run something on the compute node with the following resources:
--ntasks=1 → run the command once. A task is one copy of your command. Without this option, SLURM can start more than one copy, and you would see “Hello world” twice
--cpus-per-task=1 → request 1 CPU core
--mem=1G → request 1 GB of memory
--time=00:10:00 → set a maximum runtime of 10 minutes (hours:minutes:seconds). If the job runs longer, SLURM stops it. On Crunchomics, a job can run for at most 7 days. If you need more time, contact Wim de Leeuw. Always set a time limit, with some extra time on top of what you expect. Without --time, a job that hangs can block CPUs and memory that others could use for a long time
echo "Hello world" → the actual command to run (echo is a command that prints text to the screen)

So the arguments after srun and before echo are where you tell SLURM what resources to allocate on the compute node.
srun keeps your terminal busy until the job is done. You see the output of the job in your terminal, and then you get your prompt back. While the job runs, you can’t type other commands in this terminal. To see the job in squeue, use a second terminal that is logged in to Crunchomics.


5.3.3 Running an analysis with Seqkit interactively
Next, let’s use srun for something more useful. You will analyze the fasta files that you explored before, but now with a tool called seqkit. seqkit is a toolkit that you can use for inspecting FASTA/FASTQ files. Seqkit comes with different modules, for example the stats module, that generates basic summary statistics from sequence files and can be called with seqkit stats. It is already installed by default on Crunchomics, so you don’t need conda for using it.
Tip: Whenever you use a tool for the first time, check its help page (e.g., seqkit -h) to see all available options or check online for a manual or basic usage information.

# Create a results folder with a seqkit folder inside
mkdir -p results/seqkit 

# Run seqkit with srun
srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=5G --time=00:10:00 seqkit stats data/*fasta -Tao results/seqkit/16s_stats.tsv --threads 1

# View the results (press 'q' to exit less)
less -S results/seqkit/16s_stats.tsv 

Here:

seqkit stats data/*fasta → Use the seqkit stats module to analyse all FASTA files in the data folder ending in fasta
-Tao → options to store output in tabular format (-T), include all stats (-a), and write to file (-o)
--threads 1 → the number of CPUs that seqkit uses. Here, you use one thread (this should match --cpus-per-task=1)

Important: Whenever you submit jobs to the compute node, make sure that the number of requested CPUs/threads match with the number of CPUs used by the software

The results are stored in results/seqkit/16s_stats.tsv

This job takes only a few seconds. It is likely done before you can check it with squeue.
When you open the results file, you will, among others, see:

The number of sequences in each fasta file (num_seqs), this should match with what you saw during the CLI tutorial part
The average length of the sequences in bp (avg_len)
Additional metrics such as the minimum, maximum or total sequence length







TipTip: Choosing the right amount of resources





When starting out, choosing the right amount of CPUs, memory, or runtime can be tricky. Here are a few rules of thumb:

Start small, a lot of tools don’t need huge resources for small test runs
Check the tool’s documentation, some might list recommended resource settings
When starting out, you can begin by testing on a subset of your data first. It runs faster and helps you debug
If your job fails or runs out of memory, increase the resources gradually
Once you have a stable workflow, you can scale up

Remember: Over-requesting resources can make jobs wait longer in the queue, and can block others from running.

text:
6.2 Minimap2: Map reads to reference database
Nanopore long-read sequencing can produce reads that span nearly the entire 16S rRNA gene, making it useful for identifying microbial species. However, these long reads come with a trade-off: they have a higher error rate compared to short-read technologies.
Assume that your average read quality is Q12. The Phred score (Q) is a measure of how confident the sequencer is in each base call. The probability of a base being called incorrectly can be calculated as:
\[P=10^{-Q/10}\]
In R, you can compute this with:

Q <- 12
P_error <- 10^(-Q/10)
percent_error <- P_error * 100
message("Error rate: ", round(percent_error, 2), "%")

Error rate: 6.31%


This tells you that with a mean Phred quality of 12, each base has roughly a 6% chance of being incorrect. For a 1,500 bp 16S amplicon you expect 90 errors per sequence with such a quality score. While Nanopore long reads are useful because they capture the full 16S rRNA gene, a high level of errors can make species-level identification unreliable.
To classify your filtered Nanopore reads, you use Minimap2 to map each read against a reference database of 16S rRNA sequences from all the strains used in your lab experiments. Mapping identifies the reference sequence most similar to each read. The read is then aligned base-by-base to the corresponding reference sequence to check for exact matches or mismatches. Depending on the similarity, one or more hits may be recorded for each read.
Mapping tools like Minimap2 are well-suited for Nanopore data because they tolerate mismatches as well as small insertions and deletions, which are common in error-prone long reads. The output of Minimap2 is a PAF (Pairwise mApping Format) file, which contains information about how well each read maps to the reference sequences.
Some reads match more than one reference sequence (multi-mappers). This can happen if the strains have highly similar 16S sequences (for example the different Pseudomonas strains you worked with in the lab). These multi-mapping reads are important to keep in mind when summarizing taxonomic abundances.
minimap2 then writes one line per hit. The best hit is the primary alignment, the other hits are secondary alignments. minimap2 also gives each alignment a mapping quality. For a primary alignment, it tells you how sure minimap2 is that this is the right reference: 60 means very sure, a low value means that another reference fits almost as well. Secondary alignments always get a mapping quality of 0.
Crunchomics already has minimap2 installed. However, it is an older version (minimap2 --version prints 2.22-r1105-dirty). The word “dirty” means that it was built from a changed copy of the code, so nobody else can install exactly this version. So, like for chopper, you install a recent version with mamba:

mamba create -n minimap2_2.31 -c bioconda minimap2=2.31

6.3 Generate a count table
Now that you have your alignment results, your next goal is to summarize them into a count table, a matrix showing how many reads aligned to each reference 16S rRNA sequence. Before creating the count table, you first need to filter your results to make sure you only count high-confidence matches by:

Removing low-confidence hits by filtering out alignments with:

Low sequence identity (many mismatches)
Low coverage (only part of the read mapped to the reference)
Low mapping quality (1 to 29: minimap2 found a best hit, but another reference fits almost as well)

Selecting the single best alignment for each read (to handle multi-mappers)

Afterwards, you can count how many reads map to each reference sequence. These counts can then be summarized at higher taxonomic levels (e.g., genus) to account for the uncertainty due to sequencing errors.
The filter keeps alignments with a mapping quality of 0 on purpose. For a genus with several very similar strains, such as Pseudomonas, minimap2 often can’t tell which strain a read comes from. Keeping the secondary alignments means that the read still counts for the genus, even if the strain is unclear.
Instead of using a single pre-built program, you will use a custom Python script to perform this step. You might wonder why you use a tool like Python or R for this and not do this directly via the terminal:
Tools like Minimap2 produce large, text-based alignment files. While command-line tools are great for specific tasks (like counting lines or filtering by quality), programming languages like Python and R allow you to:

Combine multiple filtering criteria (e.g. identity, coverage, quality)
Parse complex data formats
Summarize and visualize results reproducibly

conda activate minimap2_2.31

for barcode in $(cat barcodes.txt); do
    echo "Now running minimap2: ${barcode}"

    srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=20G --time=00:30:00 minimap2 \
        -cx map-ont -t 2 \
        data/amplicons_nr.fasta \
        results/chopper/${barcode}_filtered.fastq.gz \
        > results/minimap2/${barcode}.paf
done

conda deactivate

# Task 4: check the output
wc -l barcodes.txt
ls results/chopper/*_filtered.fastq.gz | wc -l
ls results/minimap2/*.paf | wc -l
ls -lh results/chopper/ results/minimap2/
wc -l results/minimap2/*.paf

# Task 5: one seqkit file for all barcodes, then one count table
srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=5G --time=00:10:00 seqkit stats results/chopper/*_filtered.fastq.gz \
    -Tao results/seqkit/all_filtered.tsv --threads 1

less -S results/seqkit/all_filtered.tsv

conda activate python_3.10.18

mkdir results/tables_all

python scripts/paf_to_matrix.py \
  -i results/minimap2/ \
  -s results/seqkit/all_filtered.tsv \
  -t data/accession_to_genus.tsv \
  -o results/tables_all

conda deactivate

# Task 6: look at the table
less -S results/tables_all/otu_table_genus.tsv


If you see more columns than barcodes, an old .paf file is still in results/minimap2/. If you see fewer, a barcode failed in the loop. Scroll back through what the loop printed. For example, chopper printed Kept 0 reads out of 2 reads, the filtered fastq file has 20 bytes and the .paf file has 0 lines. The script then leaves that barcode out of the table.
Yes. The loop runs the same commands on the same file, so your first barcode gets the same numbers again. The new table can have extra rows with 0 for your first barcode: genera that were found only in your other barcodes.
This depends on your samples. Compare the barcodes with each other. If one barcode has many more unassigned reads than the others, look at its chopper and seqkit numbers.
You should see no warning. Warning: no seqkit stats found for: ... means that a barcode in results/minimap2/ has no row in your seqkit file. Its unassigned reads are then not counted. Warning: no reads counted for: ... means that a barcode had no reads left after filtering. It has no column in the table (see question 1).

title: 7  Using LLMs to understand and check your analysis
text:
7.1 Why learn the command line if an LLM can write the code?
This page is optional. During the tutorial, don’t use an LLM for your analysis: for questions, ask your teachers. If you finish the other chapters early, you can work through this page instead of the bonus section on loops at the end of the long-read chapter, and use UvA AI Chat for its exercises. If you do, note it in your notebook, as described in Writing down your use of an LLM in your notebook. You can also read it after the course, if you want to use LLMs later, for example in your thesis or a research project. Check first how much LLM use is allowed there. The page is about tools like UvA AI Chat, ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and how you can use them for the analysis in this tutorial and still understand what your code does.
All these tools are built on a large language model (LLM): a program that was trained on huge amounts of text, including a lot of code, and that writes an answer by predicting which words are likely to come next. On this page, I use “LLM” for all of these chat tools.
The short version:
In the tests I did for writing this page and for related tutorials, most of the LLMs’ answers were correct, but that was also a problem: the wrong ones looked just as convincing. The mistakes were often hidden in details: one option, one number, one sentence. Some of them would have changed the results without any error message: a quality cutoff that would have removed 92% of the reads, a job script that ran a quality cleaning tool without the trimming options, and means that came out too low because of empty fields. Each mistake could be caught with a basic command from this tutorial, such as ls, head, wc -l, grep or the help page of the tool. That is why it is important to learn the basics first.
Even if you use an LLM, someone still has to:
All of these need the skills you learn in this tutorial. An LLM can help with each of them, but the responsibility stays with you.

For most of you, this tutorial is the first time on a command line. That is exactly the moment to type the commands yourself, make mistakes and read the error messages. This is how you learn what “normal” looks like: a normal fastq file, a normal PAF file, a normal log file. So during the tutorial:

7.3.1 Rules at the UvA
I checked this on 6 November 2026. These rules may change, so check the linked pages yourself.

The UvA offers its own tool, UvA AI Chat. It is free with your UvAnetID, and every student gets the same features. What you type stays within the UvA environment and is not used to train models

The same page also says that the use of UvA AI Chat and other AI tools is forbidden unless your course explicitly allows it, and that you may use it to support your learning, not to do your work
The normal rules for privacy and research data also apply in the UvA AI Chat. The UvA page on responsible use says, for example, never to upload lists of names of students, patients or research participants

In this course: you may use UvA AI Chat only for the exercises on this page. Any other use of AI tools in this course is not allowed.
Everything on this page works with UvA AI Chat, with free access and only a chat window. If you use a tool that runs commands for you, the advice matters even more: you see less of what happens, so checking the result is even more important.






ImportantDon’t paste your data into an LLM





You rarely need to do this. To ask about a problem, a few lines are usually enough: the command you ran, the error message, maybe the first lines of a file, and what is special about your data (see “How to ask” below). You don’t need to upload your fastq files, your plots or your count table. Describe what you see in words instead, for example: “most reads are between 1400 and 1550 bp” or “chopper kept only 30% of my reads”.

text:
7.4 How to ask

Ask it to explain, not only to write. You can say it directly: “Explain, but do NOT give me a code solution”
Be specific. Give the one command, the exact error message and the biological context: “Nanopore reads of the full 16S rRNA gene”
Tell it what is special about your data. The LLM only knows what you tell it. It doesn’t have the full context of your analysis. Things you noted in your quality assessment change what a good answer is, for example: “my length plot has a second peak at around 700 bp”, “my barcode has only 800 reads”, “this sequencing run had a low yield” or “one of these samples is a negative control”. In tables, small details such as empty columns can change the result of a command without any error message. My AWK tutorial shows an example: one sentence, “column 4 has empty fields for missing values”, would have prevented wrong significance values. You can only add this if you know your data. That is why it is so important to look closely at your data, intermediate outputs and results
Ask one thing at a time. Long answers are hard to check. “Only explain what -q does” gives an answer you can actually test
Ask for the simplest version. LLMs tend to add extra checks and variables. That makes the code longer and harder to understand
Ask which version it describes. Tools change. Your help page (chopper -h) describes the version you actually use. If the LLM and the help page differ, the help page wins
Ask what you should check. “Which part of your answer should I check myself, and how?” is a good follow-up question

And the most important rule: if you can’t explain a step, don’t use it yet.
